newsitem.title: INDIA: India shelves Agni ballistic missile.
newsitem.headline: India shelves Agni ballistic missile.

text.p: India, under pressure from the United States to roll back its ballistic weapons programme, said on Thursday it will not produce its intermediate-range Agni missile unless the nation's security is threatened.

Analysts said the decision to shelve the surface-to-surface missile, believed capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, would help keep a lid on tension in South Asia but leave the government vulnerable to attack by domestic hardliners.
"It marks a strikingly moderate line," a diplomat said.
The decision was made public by a parliamentary committee, which released a defence ministry report prepared in October.

"Agni is a re-entry technology demonstration project which has been successfully completed and all the objectives have been met," the ministry said in a report to parliament. "Agni project did not envisage development of a missile system."

"The decision to develop and produce a missile system based on Agni technology, however, can be taken at an appropriate time consistent with the prevailing threat perception and global or regional security environment," it said.
The report was at odds with the recommendations of the all-party parliamentary panel, which had urged the government to produce the Agni for induction into the armed forces.
It also appeared to mark a shift in the government's stance.

In an August report, the defence ministry said the government was under pressure to hold off on the development of the Agni and other missiles. But it said India would "continue with its indigenous missile development programmes".

The decision to hold back on producing the missile was criticised by the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party, which has advocated a tougher line on defence than Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government.
"The development and deployment of this missile should not be delayed or stopped under pressure," BJP spokesman Krishna Lal Sharma said.

The decision was made public only days after Chinese President Jiang Zemin made an official visit to New Delhi. China and India fought a brief border war in 1962 and still disagree over parts of their Himalayan boundary.
"Coming after Jiang's visit, this is a source of embarrassment for the government," defence analyst Brahma Chellaney of the Centre for Policy Research told Reuters.
With a range of 2,500 km (1,500 miles), the Agni is considered as a potential deterrent against China. India last tested the 14-tonne, 19-metre (60-foot) Agni in 1994.
India's 250-km (150-mile) Prithvi would be more suited as a deterrent against Pakistan, analysts said.
A diplomat said: "The signal that this sends to critics of the government following Jiang's visit is that the government is pusillanimous."
The United States has urged New Delhi to halt missile testing permanently, fearing an arms race between India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since 1947.
India detonated a nuclear device in 1974 but says it has not built a nuclear bomb. The United States believes both India and Pakistan could quickly assemble nuclear weapons.

"There is the widely held perception that India's missile programme has slowed down under U.S. pressure," Chellaney said. "Basically the Agni is in hibernation because the government does not have the political will to move ahead."
